Basics

The imaginary unit

i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1i3=−ii^3 = -ii3=−ii4=1i^4 = 1i4=1

Powers of iii repeat every 4: in=i n mod 4i^n = i^{\,n \bmod 4}in=inmod4.

The idea

iii is a number whose square is −1-1−1. Multiplying by iii is a quarter turn in the plane, so the powers of iii go round in a cycle of four: 1,i,−1,−i1, i, -1, -i1,i,−1,−i. For a big power, divide the exponent by 4 and keep the remainder.

Worked example

i10i^{10}i10: 10=4⋅2+210 = 4\cdot 2 + 210=4⋅2+2, so i10=i2=−1i^{10} = i^2 = -1i10=i2=−1. And i7=i3=−ii^{7} = i^3 = -ii7=i3=−i.

Algebraic form

z=a+biz = a + biz=a+biRe⁡z=a,Im⁡z=b\operatorname{Re}z = a, \quad \operatorname{Im}z = bRez=a,Imz=b

Im⁡z\operatorname{Im} zImz is the real number bbb, without the iii.

Symbols: aaa, bbb: real numbers; iii: the imaginary unit (i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1).

The idea

A complex number is a point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) of the plane written as a+bia + bia+bi. Add like vectors; multiply like ordinary brackets, then replace i2i^2i2 by −1-1−1. Careful: the imaginary part is the real number bbb, not bibibi.

Worked example

(2+3i)(1−i)=2−2i+3i−3i2=2+i+3=5+i(2 + 3i)(1 - i) = 2 - 2i + 3i - 3i^2 = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i(2+3i)(1−i)=2−2i+3i−3i2=2+i+3=5+i. Sums are even easier: (2+3i)+(1−5i)=3−2i(2 + 3i) + (1 - 5i) = 3 - 2i(2+3i)+(1−5i)=3−2i.

Conjugate

zˉ=a−bi\bar z = a - bizˉ=a−biz+zˉ=2az + \bar z = 2az+zˉ=2az−zˉ=2biz - \bar z = 2biz−zˉ=2bi

Symbols: zˉ\bar zzˉ (“zzz bar”): the conjugate, same real part, opposite imaginary part.

The idea

The conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part: it is the mirror image of zzz in the real axis. Adding zzz and zˉ\bar zzˉ keeps only the real part (twice); subtracting keeps only the imaginary part. To solve an equation with zzz and zˉ\bar zzˉ, write z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi and compare real and imaginary parts.

Worked example

z=4−3iz = 4 - 3iz=4−3i: zˉ=4+3i\bar z = 4 + 3izˉ=4+3i, z+zˉ=8z + \bar z = 8z+zˉ=8 (real), z−zˉ=−6iz - \bar z = -6iz−zˉ=−6i (imaginary).

Modulus

∣z∣=a2+b2|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}∣z∣=a2+b2​zzˉ=∣z∣2z\bar z = |z|^2zzˉ=∣z∣2

Symbols: ∣z∣\lvert z\rvert∣z∣: the modulus, the distance from zzz to 000 in the plane.

The idea

∣z∣\lvert z\rvert∣z∣ is the distance from 0 to the point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b): Pythagoras gives a2+b2\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}a2+b2​. Multiplying zzz by its conjugate gives exactly ∣z∣2\lvert z\rvert^2∣z∣2, a real number — the key to dividing.

Worked example

∣3+4i∣=9+16=5\lvert 3 + 4i\rvert = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5∣3+4i∣=9+16​=5, and (3+4i)(3−4i)=9+16=25=52(3 + 4i)(3 - 4i) = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2(3+4i)(3−4i)=9+16=25=52.

Division

zw=z wˉ∣w∣2\frac{z}{w} = \frac{z\,\bar w}{|w|^2}wz​=∣w∣2zwˉ​

Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

The idea

To get rid of iii in the denominator, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator: the bottom becomes the real number ∣w∣2\lvert w\rvert^2∣w∣2. Then split into real and imaginary parts.

Worked example

3+4i1+2i=(3+4i)(1−2i)1+4=3−6i+4i+85=11−2i5\tfrac{3 + 4i}{1 + 2i} = \tfrac{(3 + 4i)(1 - 2i)}{1 + 4} = \tfrac{3 - 6i + 4i + 8}{5} = \tfrac{11 - 2i}{5}1+2i3+4i​=1+4(3+4i)(1−2i)​=53−6i+4i+8​=511−2i​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Rules for the modulus

∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣|zw| = |z||w|∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣\left|\frac zw\right| = \frac{|z|}{|w|}​wz​​=∣w∣∣z∣​∣z+w∣≤∣z∣+∣w∣|z + w| \le |z| + |w|∣z+w∣≤∣z∣+∣w∣

The idea

Moduli multiply and divide like ordinary numbers, so you never need to expand a product to find its modulus. For sums there is only an inequality: going from 0 to z+wz + wz+w in two steps is never shorter than the direct path (the triangle inequality).

Worked example

∣(3+4i)(5−12i)∣=5⋅13=65\lvert(3 + 4i)(5 - 12i)\rvert = 5\cdot 13 = 65∣(3+4i)(5−12i)∣=5⋅13=65, no multiplication needed. ∣(1+i)8∣=(2)8=16\lvert(1 + i)^8\rvert = (\sqrt2)^8 = 16∣(1+i)8∣=(2​)8=16.

Polar form

Polar and exponential form

z=r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)=reiθz = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = re^{i\theta}z=r(cosθ+isinθ)=reiθ

Symbols: r=∣z∣r = \lvert z\rvertr=∣z∣: the modulus; θ\thetaθ: the argument, the angle from the positive real axis.

The idea

A point can be given by its distance rrr from 0 and its angle θ\thetaθ from the positive real axis. Then a=rcos⁡θa = r\cos\thetaa=rcosθ, b=rsin⁡θb = r\sin\thetab=rsinθ, which Euler’s formula packs into reiθre^{i\theta}reiθ. Use a+bia + bia+bi to add, reiθre^{i\theta}reiθ to multiply and take powers.

Worked example

1+i1 + i1+i is at distance 2\sqrt22​ and angle π4\tfrac\pi44π​: 1+i=2 eiπ/41 + i = \sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4}1+i=2​eiπ/4. Back again: 2(cos⁡π4+isin⁡π4)=1+i\sqrt2(\cos\tfrac\pi4 + i\sin\tfrac\pi4) = 1 + i2​(cos4π​+isin4π​)=1+i.

Modulus and argument

r=∣z∣r = |z|r=∣z∣tan⁡θ=ba\tan\theta = \frac batanθ=ab​

Check the quadrant of (a, b) before choosing θ.

Symbols: z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi; θ\thetaθ: the argument.

The idea

tan⁡θ=ba\tan\theta = \tfrac batanθ=ab​ alone is ambiguous: 1+i1 + i1+i and −1−i-1 - i−1−i have the same ratio. Always place the point first: find the reference angle from ∣ba∣\lvert\tfrac ba\rvert∣ab​∣, then adjust it to the quadrant of (a,b)(a, b)(a,b).

Worked example

z=−1+3iz = -1 + \sqrt3 iz=−1+3​i: r=1+3=2r = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2r=1+3​=2; the reference angle is π3\tfrac\pi33π​, and the point is in quadrant II, so θ=π−π3=2π3\theta = \pi - \tfrac\pi3 = \tfrac{2\pi}3θ=π−3π​=32π​.

Euler’s formula

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θe^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\thetaeiθ=cosθ+isinθeiπ+1=0e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0eiπ+1=0

Symbols: e≈2.718e \approx 2.718e≈2.718: Euler’s number; θ\thetaθ in radians.

The idea

eiθe^{i\theta}eiθ is the point of the unit circle at angle θ\thetaθ. So exponentials of imaginary numbers just go round the circle, and multiplying them adds the angles. At θ=π\theta = \piθ=π you get the famous eiπ=−1e^{i\pi} = -1eiπ=−1.

Worked example

eiπ/2=cos⁡π2+isin⁡π2=ie^{i\pi/2} = \cos\tfrac\pi2 + i\sin\tfrac\pi2 = ieiπ/2=cos2π​+isin2π​=i and e2πi=1e^{2\pi i} = 1e2πi=1: a full turn brings you back.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Product and quotient

r1eiθ1⋅r2eiθ2=r1r2 ei(θ1+θ2)r_1e^{i\theta_1}\cdot r_2e^{i\theta_2} = r_1r_2\,e^{i(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}r1​eiθ1​⋅r2​eiθ2​=r1​r2​ei(θ1​+θ2​)r1eiθ1r2eiθ2=r1r2ei(θ1−θ2)\frac{r_1e^{i\theta_1}}{r_2e^{i\theta_2}} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}e^{i(\theta_1 - \theta_2)}r2​eiθ2​r1​eiθ1​​=r2​r1​​ei(θ1​−θ2​)

Multiply the moduli, add the arguments.

The idea

In polar form, multiplication is “stretch and turn”: the moduli multiply and the arguments add. Division undoes it: divide the moduli, subtract the arguments. Much quicker than expanding brackets.

Worked example

(2eiπ/6)(3eiπ/3)=6eiπ/2=6i(2e^{i\pi/6})(3e^{i\pi/3}) = 6e^{i\pi/2} = 6i(2eiπ/6)(3eiπ/3)=6eiπ/2=6i: modulus 2⋅32\cdot 32⋅3, argument π6+π3\tfrac\pi6 + \tfrac\pi36π​+3π​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Cosine and sine from exponentials

cos⁡θ=eiθ+e−iθ2\cos\theta = \frac{e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}}{2}cosθ=2eiθ+e−iθ​sin⁡θ=eiθ−e−iθ2i\sin\theta = \frac{e^{i\theta} - e^{-i\theta}}{2i}sinθ=2ieiθ−e−iθ​

The idea

eiθe^{i\theta}eiθ and e−iθe^{-i\theta}e−iθ are mirror images: adding them cancels the imaginary parts, subtracting cancels the real parts. This turns trigonometry into algebra — useful to linearise powers like cos⁡3θ\cos^3\thetacos3θ.

Worked example

cos⁡2θ=(eiθ+e−iθ2)2=e2iθ+2+e−2iθ4=1+cos⁡2θ2\cos^2\theta = \left(\tfrac{e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{e^{2i\theta} + 2 + e^{-2i\theta}}{4} = \tfrac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}cos2θ=(2eiθ+e−iθ​)2=4e2iθ+2+e−2iθ​=21+cos2θ​ — the power-lowering formula, recovered by algebra.

Powers and roots

De Moivre

(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n=cos⁡nθ+isin⁡nθ(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta(cosθ+isinθ)n=cosnθ+isinnθ

The idea

Raising a point of the unit circle to the power nnn multiplies its angle by nnn — it is (eiθ)n=einθ(e^{i\theta})^n = e^{in\theta}(eiθ)n=einθ written with cosines and sines. Expanding the left side gives formulas for cos⁡nθ\cos n\thetacosnθ and sin⁡nθ\sin n\thetasinnθ.

Worked example

(cos⁡π6+isin⁡π6)6=cos⁡π+isin⁡π=−1\left(\cos\tfrac\pi6 + i\sin\tfrac\pi6\right)^6 = \cos\pi + i\sin\pi = -1(cos6π​+isin6π​)6=cosπ+isinπ=−1: six steps of 30∘30^\circ30∘ make a half turn.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Powers

zn=rneinθz^n = r^n e^{in\theta}zn=rneinθ

The idea

To raise zzz to a power, go to polar form: the modulus is raised to the power, the argument is multiplied. (1+i)10(1 + i)^{10}(1+i)10 by expanding would be painful; in polar form it takes two lines.

Worked example

(1+i)8=(2 eiπ/4)8=16 e2πi=16(1 + i)^8 = (\sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4})^8 = 16\,e^{2\pi i} = 16(1+i)8=(2​eiπ/4)8=16e2πi=16.

n-th roots

zk=rn  eiθ+2kπnz_k = \sqrt[n]{r}\;e^{i\frac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}}zk​=nr​einθ+2kπ​k=0,1,…,n−1k = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1k=0,1,…,n−1

The n roots form a regular polygon around 0.

Symbols: rrr, θ\thetaθ: modulus and argument of zzz; zkz_kzk​: the nnn roots.

The idea

zzz has exactly nnn different nnn-th roots. All have modulus rn\sqrt[n]{r}nr​; their arguments are θn\tfrac{\theta}{n}nθ​ plus multiples of 2πn\tfrac{2\pi}{n}n2π​. So they sit evenly on a circle, the vertices of a regular nnn-gon.

Worked example

The cube roots of 8: modulus 83=2\sqrt[3]8 = 238​=2, arguments 0,2π3,4π30, \tfrac{2\pi}3, \tfrac{4\pi}30,32π​,34π​: 222, −1+3i-1 + \sqrt3 i−1+3​i, −1−3i-1 - \sqrt3 i−1−3​i — an equilateral triangle.

Roots of unity

ωk=e2πik/n\omega_k = e^{2\pi i k/n}ωk​=e2πik/n∑k=0n−1ωk=0\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\omega_k = 0k=0∑n−1​ωk​=0

Symbols: ωk\omega_kωk​: the nnn solutions of zn=1z^n = 1zn=1.

The idea

The nnn-th roots of 1 are nnn equally spaced points on the unit circle, starting at 1. Pulling in nnn directions with equal force, they balance: their sum is 0.

Worked example

The 4th roots of unity are 1,i,−1,−i1, i, -1, -i1,i,−1,−i: they add to 0, and each is a power of iii.

Cube roots of unity

ω=−12+32i\omega = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}iω=−21​+23​​i1+ω+ω2=01 + \omega + \omega^2 = 01+ω+ω2=0ω3=1\omega^3 = 1ω3=1

Symbols: ω\omegaω (omega): a complex solution of z3=1z^3 = 1z3=1.

The idea

z3=1z^3 = 1z3=1 factors as (z−1)(z2+z+1)=0(z - 1)(z^2 + z + 1) = 0(z−1)(z2+z+1)=0, so besides 1 there are two roots ω\omegaω and ω2=ωˉ\omega^2 = \bar\omegaω2=ωˉ, solving z2+z+1=0z^2 + z + 1 = 0z2+z+1=0. That gives 1+ω+ω2=01 + \omega + \omega^2 = 01+ω+ω2=0, the identity behind many simplifications.

Worked example

ω100=ω99⋅ω=(ω3)33ω=ω\omega^{100} = \omega^{99}\cdot\omega = (\omega^3)^{33}\omega = \omegaω100=ω99⋅ω=(ω3)33ω=ω. And ω2+ω=−1\omega^2 + \omega = -1ω2+ω=−1 straight from the identity.

Geometry in the complex plane

Distance

d(z1,z2)=∣z1−z2∣d(z_1, z_2) = |z_1 - z_2|d(z1​,z2​)=∣z1​−z2​∣

The idea

z1−z2z_1 - z_2z1​−z2​ is the vector from z2z_2z2​ to z1z_1z1​, so its modulus is the distance between the two points. Many geometry questions become moduli of differences.

Worked example

1+2i1 + 2i1+2i and 4+6i4 + 6i4+6i: the difference is 3+4i3 + 4i3+4i, so the distance is 5.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Circle

∣z−z0∣=r|z - z_0| = r∣z−z0​∣=r

Symbols: z0z_0z0​: the centre, rrr: the radius.

The idea

∣z−z0∣=r\lvert z - z_0\rvert = r∣z−z0​∣=r: all points at distance rrr from z0z_0z0​, a circle. Read the centre carefully: ∣z−1+2i∣=∣z−(1−2i)∣\lvert z - 1 + 2i\rvert = \lvert z - (1 - 2i)\rvert∣z−1+2i∣=∣z−(1−2i)∣, so the centre is 1−2i1 - 2i1−2i. With <<< instead of === you get the inside disc.

Worked example

∣z−(2+i)∣=3\lvert z - (2 + i)\rvert = 3∣z−(2+i)∣=3 is the circle with centre 2+i2 + i2+i and radius 3. In coordinates: (x−2)2+(y−1)2=9(x - 2)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 9(x−2)2+(y−1)2=9.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Perpendicular bisector

∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣|z - a| = |z - b|∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣

Symbols: The points zzz equally far from aaa and bbb.

The idea

∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣\lvert z - a\rvert = \lvert z - b\rvert∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣: the points equally far from aaa and bbb. That is the perpendicular bisector of the segment ababab — a straight line through its midpoint, at right angles to it.

Worked example

∣z−2∣=∣z+2∣\lvert z - 2\rvert = \lvert z + 2\rvert∣z−2∣=∣z+2∣: points equally far from 222 and −2-2−2, so the imaginary axis Re⁡z=0\operatorname{Re}z = 0Rez=0.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Rotation

z↦eiθzz \mapsto e^{i\theta}zz↦eiθz

Multiplying by i rotates by 90°.

The idea

Multiplying by eiθe^{i\theta}eiθ keeps the modulus (it is 1) and adds θ\thetaθ to the argument: a rotation by θ\thetaθ about 0. Multiplying by iii is a quarter turn: (a+bi)i=−b+ai(a + bi)i = -b + ai(a+bi)i=−b+ai.

Worked example

(3+i)⋅i=3i+i2=−1+3i(3 + i)\cdot i = 3i + i^2 = -1 + 3i(3+i)⋅i=3i+i2=−1+3i: the point (3,1)(3, 1)(3,1) turns to (−1,3)(-1, 3)(−1,3), a right angle further, same distance from 0.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Conjugate

z↦zˉz \mapsto \bar zz↦zˉ

Reflection in the real axis.

The idea

z↦zˉz \mapsto \bar zz↦zˉ flips the sign of the imaginary part: the reflection in the real axis. Points on the real axis stay put (zˉ=z\bar z = zzˉ=z means zzz is real); points on the imaginary axis are sent to their opposites.

Worked example

Reflecting 3+2i3 + 2i3+2i gives 3−2i3 - 2i3−2i; reflecting 5i5i5i gives −5i-5i−5i; 777 stays 777.

Polynomials

Quadratic with Δ < 0

x=−b±i−Δ2ax = \frac{-b \pm i\sqrt{-\Delta}}{2a}x=2a−b±i−Δ​​

Symbols: Δ=b2−4ac<0\Delta = b^2 - 4ac < 0Δ=b2−4ac<0, so −Δ\sqrt{-\Delta}−Δ​ is real.

The idea

When the discriminant is negative the parabola misses the xxx-axis, but the equation still has two roots: complex conjugates. Use the usual formula with Δ=i−Δ\sqrt{\Delta} = i\sqrt{-\Delta}Δ​=i−Δ​.

Worked example

x2+2x+5=0x^2 + 2x + 5 = 0x2+2x+5=0: Δ=4−20=−16\Delta = 4 - 20 = -16Δ=4−20=−16, so x=−2±4i2=−1±2ix = \tfrac{-2 \pm 4i}{2} = -1 \pm 2ix=2−2±4i​=−1±2i. In the plane the two roots are mirror images.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Conjugate roots

P(z)=0 ⇒ P(zˉ)=0P(z) = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ P(\bar z) = 0P(z)=0 ⇒ P(zˉ)=0

Polynomials with real coefficients have non-real roots in conjugate pairs.

The idea

If the coefficients are real, conjugating the equation P(z)=0P(z) = 0P(z)=0 changes nothing except zzz into zˉ\bar zzˉ. So non-real roots come in conjugate pairs, and each pair gives a real quadratic factor z2−2Re⁡(z) z+∣z∣2z^2 - 2\operatorname{Re}(z)\,z + \lvert z\rvert^2z2−2Re(z)z+∣z∣2.

Worked example

A real cubic has root 1+i1 + i1+i: then 1−i1 - i1−i is also a root, and (z−1−i)(z−1+i)=z2−2z+2(z - 1 - i)(z - 1 + i) = z^2 - 2z + 2(z−1−i)(z−1+i)=z2−2z+2 divides the cubic.

Fundamental theorem of algebra

deg⁡P=n ⇒ P(z)=an(z−z1)⋯(z−zn)\deg P = n \ \Rightarrow\ P(z) = a_n(z - z_1)\cdots(z - z_n)degP=n ⇒ P(z)=an​(z−z1​)⋯(z−zn​)

Counted with multiplicity.

Symbols: z1,…,znz_1, \dots, z_nz1​,…,zn​: the roots; ana_nan​: the leading coefficient; deg⁡P\deg PdegP: the degree.

The idea

Over the complex numbers every polynomial of degree nnn splits completely into nnn linear factors: it has exactly nnn roots, counting repeated ones. In the reals some of them may be missing — that is why complex numbers were invented.

Worked example

z4−1=(z−1)(z+1)(z−i)(z+i)z^4 - 1 = (z - 1)(z + 1)(z - i)(z + i)z4−1=(z−1)(z+1)(z−i)(z+i): degree 4, four roots — only two of them real.
